body:
The emergence of modern literature

Modern Indian literature developed rapidly during the 19th century under the combined influence of printing, colonial education, social reform, contact with Western literature and the growth of Indian nationalism. Writers increasingly addressed contemporary society, individual experiences, social inequalities and the political condition of India.

Modern literature did not completely replace earlier literary traditions. Indian languages already possessed rich traditions of poetry, devotional literature, storytelling and philosophical writing. Modern writers adapted these traditions while developing new forms of prose, fiction, journalism and political expression.

Development of printing in India

Before the widespread use of printing, manuscripts were copied by hand on palm leaves or handmade paper. This made their production relatively expensive and limited their circulation. Printing enabled publishers to produce numerous copies of the same text and distribute them across different regions.

YearDevelopmentSignificance
1556Printing press established at Old Goa by Jesuit missionariesBeginning of European-style printing in India
1780Hicky's Bengal Gazette, CalcuttaFirst English newspaper published in India
1810Printed edition of Ramcharitmanas, CalcuttaWider circulation of vernacular religious literature
1822Bombay SamacharLandmark in Gujarati journalism

Missionaries initially used printing mainly for religious instruction. Over time, Indian reformers, journalists, educational institutions and commercial publishers adopted printing for a much wider range of purposes.

Formation of a reading public

Cheaper books, newspapers, magazines and pamphlets created opportunities for people outside traditional scholarly circles to participate in literary and intellectual life. Printed works also reached people who could not read through collective readings and oral recitation.

The development of vernacular literature, meaning literature in languages commonly used by people in particular regions, allowed writers to discuss contemporary problems in familiar languages. Translations enabled ideas and literary forms to travel between linguistic communities.

Important forms of modern literature

Literary formPrincipal feature
NovelExtended fictional narrative portraying characters and society
Short storyBrief fictional narrative concentrating on a limited experience or situation
DramaLiterary composition presenting events through characters and dialogue
Essay and pamphletDirect discussion of social, religious or political questions
AutobiographyAccount of a person's life written by that person
Patriotic poetryExpression of attachment to the homeland, collective identity or freedom
JournalismPublic communication of news, opinions and contemporary issues

These forms frequently overlapped in their purposes. A novel could advocate social reform, a poem could encourage political resistance, and a newspaper could publish literary works alongside political commentary.

Printing encouraged modern literature, but it did not create Indian literary traditions from nothing. Earlier manuscripts, oral narratives and regional poetry continued to influence modern writing.

Prelims focus

  • 1556: Jesuit missionaries established a printing press in Goa.
  • 1780: James Augustus Hicky published the Bengal Gazette.
  • 1822: Bombay Samachar began publication.
  • Printing encouraged vernacular literature and wider public discussion.
  • Trap: Modern Indian literature developed in regional languages as well as English.

[References: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, Print Culture and the Modern World, pp. 167–175; Government of Goa, Department of Printing and Stationery, About Us: History of Press Technology in Goa; Press Information Bureau, Evolution of PIB. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Print Culture and the Rise of Modern Indian Literature

body:
Newspapers as instruments of public debate

During the 19th century, newspapers became an important means of discussing social customs, religious beliefs, economic conditions and colonial policies. Reformers used newspapers to persuade readers, while opponents of reform established publications to defend existing traditions.

The resulting debates helped create a public sphere, in which questions previously discussed within limited social or religious circles could reach a much larger audience.

Reform-oriented publications

PublicationAssociated personalityPrincipal orientation
Sambad KaumudiRaja Rammohun RoyBengali newspaper supporting social reform from 1821
Samachar ChandrikaOrthodox Hindu opinionOpposition to reformist positions associated with Rammohun Roy
Rast GoftarDadabhai NaorojiSocial reform, particularly within the Parsi community
Satya PrakashKarsandas MuljiGujarati social and religious reform

The debate between Sambad Kaumudi and Samachar Chandrika illustrates an important feature of print culture: printing could spread both progressive and conservative ideas. It provided a means of public argument rather than guaranteeing agreement.

The growth of nationalist journalism

As political consciousness developed, newspapers increasingly criticised colonial administration, economic exploitation and restrictions on civil liberties. They carried information about political meetings, protests and nationalist movements from one region to another.

PublicationAssociationLanguage or feature
KesariBal Gangadhar TilakMarathi nationalist journalism
Amrita Bazar PatrikaSisir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal GhoshOriginally Bengali; later published in English
Young IndiaMahatma GandhiEnglish-language political and ethical discussion
NavajivanMahatma GandhiGujarati communication of Gandhian ideas

The Vernacular Press Act, 1878

The British colonial government became increasingly concerned about criticism appearing in Indian-language newspapers. The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 provided extensive powers to control publications in Indian languages.

The law was modelled on Irish press legislation. Authorities could issue warnings against publications considered objectionable and seize presses and confiscate printing machinery if warnings were ignored.

Unlike English-language publications, the vernacular press was specifically subjected to these restrictions. Amrita Bazar Patrika responded by changing to English publication.

Colonial censorship did not eliminate nationalist journalism. Newspapers continued to criticise British rule, and attempts to suppress them often generated further public opposition. Tilak's imprisonment in 1908 following prosecution connected with his writings in Kesari illustrates the conflict between political journalism and colonial authority.

Reformist and nationalist journalism

Reformist journalism primarily challenged inequalities and undesirable social practices within Indian society. Nationalist journalism primarily challenged colonial domination. Individual newspapers and writers could pursue both objectives.

Prelims focus

  • Sambad Kaumudi: Rammohun Roy, 1821.
  • Samachar Chandrika opposed reformist opinion.
  • Kesari: Tilak and Marathi journalism.
  • Vernacular Press Act: 1878, directed against the Indian-language press.
  • Satya Prakash: Karsandas Mulji.
  • Trap: Kesari was not an English-language newspaper.

[References: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, Print Culture and the Modern World, pp. 169–175; The Indian Express, A pre-Independence history of press freedom in India, 2017; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries on Karsandas Mulji and Gujarati journalism; Press Information Bureau, Gandhi Heritage Portal backgrounder, 2013, Journals section. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Nationalist journalism and colonial censorship

title: Reformist Journalism, Nationalist Newspapers and Press Censorship

body:
Literature as an instrument of social change

Modern Indian reformers used books, essays, pamphlets, autobiographies and fiction to challenge practices such as sati, child marriage, restrictions on widow remarriage, denial of women's education and caste discrimination.

Some reformers interpreted religious texts to demonstrate that harmful practices lacked legitimate scriptural justification. Others questioned established social authority more fundamentally and argued for equality, education and individual dignity.

Early reformist writing

Raja Rammohun Roy published arguments against sati and supported educational and religious reform. His campaign contributed to the intellectual and social conditions in which sati was prohibited in 1829.

Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar used scriptural arguments to support Hindu widow remarriage. His reform campaign contributed to the enactment of the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856.

These examples demonstrate how written argument could influence public opinion and contribute to demands for legal change.

Women as authors and reformers

Women increasingly wrote about their own experiences instead of appearing only as subjects in literature written by men. Autobiographies, essays and fictional narratives exposed restrictions on education, freedom and personal choice.

AuthorWorkCentral theme
Rashsundari DebiAmar JibanBengali autobiography describing her life and struggle to become literate
Tarabai ShindeStri Purush Tulana, 1882Marathi critique of unequal standards for men and women
Pandita RamabaiThe High-Caste Hindu Woman, 1887Oppression and hardship experienced by women, especially widows
Begum Rokeya Sakhawat HossainSultana's Dream, 1905English-language satire imagining a society governed by women

Amar Jiban is recognised as a pioneering full-length Bengali autobiography. Its importance lies in presenting women's domestic experiences and the obstacles to female literacy from the perspective of a woman who experienced them.

Begum Rokeya's Sultana's Dream used an imaginary society to question supposedly natural differences between the social roles of men and women. This is an example of reform through satire and imaginative fiction rather than direct autobiography.

Anti-caste literature

Jyotirao Phule's Gulamgiri, published in 1873, criticised caste hierarchy and hereditary social inequality. The title means slavery. Phule dedicated the work to those in the United States who had struggled against slavery, connecting the Indian struggle against caste oppression with a wider struggle for human equality.

In the 20th century, B. R. Ambedkar's writings challenged caste discrimination and questioned whether genuine social equality could exist while caste hierarchy remained intact. His Annihilation of Caste, published in 1936, is an important example of direct intellectual criticism of the caste system.

Social reform literature and nationalist literature are related but not identical. The demand for political freedom from foreign rule does not automatically resolve inequalities within society. Reformist writers therefore also examined the meaning of freedom for women and oppressed communities.

Prelims focus

  • Gulamgiri, 1873: Jyotirao Phule.
  • Stri Purush Tulana, 1882: Tarabai Shinde.
  • The High-Caste Hindu Woman, 1887: Pandita Ramabai.
  • Sultana's Dream, 1905: Begum Rokeya.
  • Annihilation of Caste, 1936: B. R. Ambedkar.
  • Trap: Amar Jiban is an autobiography, whereas Sultana's Dream is imaginative fiction.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, Women, Caste and Reform, pp. 95–108; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, Print Culture and the Modern World, pp. 172–174; Telangana SCERT, Social Studies, Class 8, 2022–23 edition, Social and Religious Reform Movements, p. 159; Dr. B. R. Ambedkar University Delhi, Political Speeches and Writings by Literary Writers, primary reading list. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of social realism

Social realism is an approach to literature that portrays ordinary people's lives and the social and economic conditions affecting them, including poverty, inequality, exploitation and discrimination.

Realist literature does not require every character or incident to be historically true. A fictional narrative can be realistic when it presents believable characters, social relationships and material conditions.

During colonial rule, social realism helped writers examine the consequences of landlordism, indebtedness, unequal social status, colonial economic policies and restrictions on women.

Dinabandhu Mitra and the indigo cultivators

Dinabandhu Mitra's Bengali play Nil Darpan, published in 1860, exposed the exploitation of indigo cultivators by European indigo planters. Its title means The Indigo Mirror.

The drama brought the problems of rural Bengal into public discussion. It demonstrates how literary writing could connect economic exploitation with criticism of colonial rule.

Premchand and Hindi-Urdu social realism

Munshi Premchand, whose original name was Dhanpat Rai, wrote in both Urdu and Hindi. He made peasants, workers, women and socially marginalised people central characters in modern Indian fiction.

WorkCentral subject
SevasadanWomen's social position, marriage, dowry and respectability
RangbhoomiDisplacement, industrial expansion and the resistance of an oppressed individual
Godan, 1936Peasant indebtedness, poverty and exploitation

In Rangbhoomi, the character Surdas resists the acquisition of his land for industrial development. The novel draws attention to the conflict between economic expansion and the interests of vulnerable people.

In Godan, Hori and Dhania represent the struggles of a peasant household burdened by debt, social obligations and economic inequality. The novel portrays rural exploitation as the result of interconnected social and economic pressures rather than an isolated personal failure.

Social realism in other languages

  • Fakir Mohan Senapati: His Odia novel Chha Mana Atha Guntha, translated as Six Acres and a Third, depicts land appropriation, rural inequality and exploitation.
  • Potheri Kunjambu: His Malayalam novel Saraswativijayam, published in 1892, questions caste oppression and emphasises the transformative importance of education.
  • Mulk Raj Anand: His English novels Untouchable and Coolie portray caste exclusion and economic exploitation respectively.

The Progressive Writers' Association

The Progressive Writers' Association encouraged literature concerned with contemporary social conditions, inequality and exploitation. Its first major all-India conference was held at Lucknow in 1936, with Premchand delivering the presidential address.

The movement brought together writers working in different Indian languages, especially Urdu and Hindi. It strengthened the connection between literary expression, social criticism and demands for change.

Realism and historical fiction

Social realism focuses on believable social conditions, while historical fiction places its narrative in an earlier historical period. A historical novel can contain realistic social observations, and a contemporary realist novel can criticise colonial rule. These categories are not mutually exclusive.

Prelims focus

  • Nil Darpan, 1860: Dinabandhu Mitra, Bengali drama.
  • Premchand wrote in both Hindi and Urdu.
  • Godan, 1936: Hori, Dhania and peasant exploitation.
  • Chha Mana Atha Guntha: Fakir Mohan Senapati, Odia.
  • Progressive Writers' Association conference: Lucknow, 1936, Premchand.
  • Trap: Nil Darpan is a play, not a novel.

[References: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, Novels, Society and History, pp. 188–199; Museums of India, Victoria Memorial Hall, Dinabandhu Mitra, accession R9081; University of California Press, Six Acres and a Third, book description; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, The Life and Work of Mulk Raj Anand; Oxford University Press, The Progressive Cultural Movement in India, Introduction. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
